title: The present tense: work, study and languages
objectives: I can conjugate verbs of both conjugations in the present tense and tell from the 'ти' form which conjugation a verb follows.
I can say where I live and work, what I am doing now and which languages I speak, and how well.
I can ask questions with 'як' and 'чому́' and answer them with adverbs and with 'тому́ що'.
I can say what I love doing with 'люби́ти' and an infinitive.
I can explain the 'л' of 'роблю́', the 'ш' of 'пишу́', the stem of 'живу́' and the stress that moves between 'пишу́' and 'пи́шеш'.

vocabulary.note: Present 'працю́ю', 'працю́єш': the suffix '-юва-' becomes '-ю-', and the stress falls on that 'ю' in every present form. It means to have a job and to work at something.
Regular, like 'чита́ти': 'зна́ю', 'зна́єш', 'зна́ють'. 'Я не зна́ю.' is the everyday way to say 'I don't know'.
Present 'живу́', 'живе́ш': the present stem 'жив-' does not show in the infinitive, and the stress stays on the ending in every present form. It means to live somewhere and to be alive.
Present 'пишу́', 'пи́шеш': the 'с' becomes 'ш' in every present form, and only the 'я' form is stressed on the ending.
Present 'розумі́ю', 'розумі́єш'. It ends in '-іти' but follows the first conjugation, like 'чита́ти'. 'Розумі́ю.' alone means 'I see'.
Regular, like 'чита́ти'. 'Слу́хаю.' alone, literally 'I-listen', is a common way to answer the phone or to tell someone to go ahead.
Regular, like 'чита́ти'. In 'Я ду́маю, що так.' the word 'що' joins a statement to the verb as English 'that' does, and 'так' is the 'yes' you know.
Present 'роблю́', 'ро́биш', 'ро́блять': second conjugation, with an 'л' added in the 'я' and 'вони́' forms. One verb covers both English 'do' and 'make'.
Present 'люблю́', 'лю́биш', 'лю́блять', with the same added 'л' as 'роби́ти'. Followed by an infinitive it says what you like or love doing.
Made from the adjective 'пога́ний', bad. It is the opposite of 'до́бре', well.
One word for 'a little' or 'a bit'. 'Тро́хи.' alone is a modest answer to 'Do you speak Ukrainian?'.
Before an adjective or adverb it means 'very' ('ду́же до́бре'); before a verb it means 'very much' or 'really' ('ду́же люблю́').
Made from the adjective 'шви́дкий', quick.
Made from the adjective 'пові́льний', slow. The opposite of 'шви́дко'.
With a present verb it shows that the action is happening at this moment, which English shows with a form of 'be' and '-ing'.
The same 'як' as in 'Як спра́ви?'. It asks in what way or how well something is done.

example.source: How well does he speak Ukrainian?

vocabulary.note: It asks for a reason. It has the same spelling as the dative question 'чому́?', to what?, from unit 5, but here it is an adverb meaning 'why'.
Two words that work as one conjunction. Inside a sentence a comma goes before them.

example.target: Я тут, тому́ що тут працю́ю.
example.source: I'm here because I work here.
example.source_literal: I here, for-that-reason that here I-work.

vocabulary.note: The instrumental feminine of the adjective 'украї́нський', agreeing with the word 'мо́вою', by language, which is left out. It is not an adverb. Learn it whole with 'говори́ти', 'писа́ти' and 'чита́ти'.
The instrumental feminine of the adjective 'англі́йський', built like 'украї́нською'. It is not an adverb.

dialogues.title: Which languages do you speak?
dialogues.context: Oksana and Sam sit in a café near the university after a lecture. They are friends and call each other 'ти'. Oksana ends her first question with 'так?', yes?, as an English speaker might end one with 'right?'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Sam, you speak English, right?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, я кана́дець. Я говорю́ англі́йською.
lines.source: Yes, I'm Canadian. I speak English.
lines.source_literal: yes, I Canadian. I speak by-English.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: And Ukrainian? You speak well!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, я говорю́ тро́хи й пові́льно.
lines.source: No, I speak a little, and slowly.
lines.source_literal: no, I speak a-little and slowly.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: But you understand well.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, я розумі́ю, але́ ти гово́риш ду́же шви́дко.
lines.source: Yes, I understand, but you speak very fast.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ви́бач! А за́раз? Я говорю́ пові́льно.
lines.source: Sorry! And now? I'm speaking slowly.
lines.source_literal: sorry! and now? I speak slowly.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: That's fine now. Thank you!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: And do you write in Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Пишу́, але́ пові́льно, тому́ що ду́маю.
lines.source: I do, but slowly, because I'm thinking.
lines.source_literal: I-write, but slowly, for-that-reason that I-think.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Do you think in English?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так. Але́ сього́дні я ду́маю украї́нською!
lines.source: Yes. But today I'm thinking in Ukrainian!
lines.source_literal: yes. but today I think by-Ukrainian!

dialogues.title: What does a programmer do?
dialogues.context: At Andrii's café, Taras meets Iryna Petrivna, Sam's teacher. They do not know each other well, so they say 'ви'. Taras is a programmer; the word for a man in that job is 'програмі́ст'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: So where do you work, Taras?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я працю́ю тут, у Ки́єві. Я програмі́ст.
lines.source: I work here, in Kyiv. I'm a programmer.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: A programmer? And what do you do?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: I think and I write.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Do you write in Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: No, in English. But I think in Ukrainian!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: And do you speak English well?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: I write it well, but I speak it badly.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Why?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тому́ що я пишу́ англі́йською, а говорю́ украї́нською.
lines.source: Because I write in English, but I speak Ukrainian.
lines.source_literal: for-that-reason that I write by-English, while I-speak by-Ukrainian.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Розумі́ю. Я вчи́телька, я працю́ю в шко́лі.
lines.source: I see. I'm a teacher; I work at a school.
lines.source_literal: I-understand. I teacher, I work in school.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я зна́ю. Сем до́бре гово́рить украї́нською!
lines.source: I know. Sam speaks Ukrainian well!
lines.source_literal: I know. Sam well speaks by-Ukrainian!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Yes, well. But slowly!

dialogues.title: Why do you love it?
dialogues.context: Taras visits his sister Olena, a doctor, one evening. She is reading. Brother and sister call each other 'ти'. 'Програмі́сти' is the plural of the word 'програмі́ст', programmer.

lines.speaker: Тара́с

lines.speaker: Оле́на

lines.source_literal: for-that-reason that books interesting. and what you like to-do?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: I love talking!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.source: Yes, I know.

lines.speaker: Тара́с

grammar.title: The present tense and the first conjugation
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian has one present tense, and it does the work of both English presents. 'Я чита́ю.' means 'I read' and also 'I am reading'. English builds the second meaning from a form of 'be' plus a form in '-ing'; Ukrainian has no such form, so the context, or a word such as 'за́раз', now, shows that something is happening at this moment: 'Я за́раз чита́ю.', 'I am reading now'.

Unit 6 showed that a present form is a stem plus a personal ending, and that verbs fall into two families, each with its own set of endings. Such a family is called a conjugation. This note covers the first conjugation. Its endings have two spellings, because the letters 'ю' and 'є' after a vowel write [j] plus a vowel (unit 3):

- after a consonant: '-у', '-еш', '-е', '-емо', '-ете', '-уть'
- after a vowel: '-ю', '-єш', '-є', '-ємо', '-єте', '-ють'

To find the present stem of most first-conjugation verbs, remove '-ти' from the infinitive. The stem of 'чита́ти' is 'чита-', which ends in a vowel, so it takes the second spelling. 'Зна́ти', 'слу́хати', 'ду́мати' and 'розумі́ти' work the same way: 'зна́ю', 'слу́хаєш', 'ду́має', 'розумі́ємо'.

Three kinds of first-conjugation verb change their stem in the present, and the 'я' form shows the change:

- Verbs in '-ува́ти' or '-юва́ти' replace the suffix '-ува-' or '-юва-' with '-у-' or '-ю-'. A suffix is a part added to a root to build a word. 'Працюва́ти' becomes 'працю́ю', 'працю́єш': the new stem 'працю-' ends in a vowel, so the endings with 'ю' and 'є' follow. The spelling '-юва-' is used after a soft consonant, as the 'ц' is here.
- 'Жи́ти' has the present stem 'жив-', which the infinitive does not show: 'живу́', 'живе́ш'. The stem ends in a consonant, so the endings are '-у', '-еш'.
- 'Писа́ти' changes 'с' to 'ш' in every present form: 'пишу́', 'пи́шеш', 'пи́шуть'.

Because the stem can change, this course gives the 'я' and 'ти' forms of every verb that does not simply drop '-ти'. The rest of the tense follows from those two. The pronoun can be left out, since the ending already shows the person: 'Пишу́.' is a complete sentence, 'I am writing'.

grammar.title: The second conjugation, choosing the conjugation, and stress
grammar.explanation:
The second conjugation has its own endings. Where the first conjugation has 'е' or 'є', the second has 'и', or 'ї' after a vowel, and where the first has '-уть' or '-ють', the second has '-ать' or '-ять':

- after a consonant: '-у' or '-ю', '-иш', '-ить', '-имо', '-ите', '-ать' or '-ять'
- after a vowel: '-ю', '-їш', '-їть', '-їмо', '-їте', '-ять'

Few second-conjugation stems end in a vowel. One is 'стоя́ти', to stand: 'стою́', 'стої́ш', 'стої́ть', 'стоя́ть'.

The model from unit 6 is 'говори́ти': remove '-ити' to get the present stem 'говор-', then add the endings: 'говорю́', 'гово́риш', 'гово́рить', 'гово́римо', 'гово́рите', 'гово́рять'. The 'я' and 'вони́' endings, spelled with 'ю' and 'я', make the consonant before them soft (unit 3), so the 'р' is soft in 'говорю́' and 'гово́рять' and hard in the other forms.

The consonants 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' cannot be fully soft in Ukrainian (unit 3). When a second-conjugation stem ends in one of them, the 'я' and 'вони́' forms add an 'л' after it, and the 'л' takes the softness instead: 'роби́ти' gives 'роблю́' and 'ро́блять', and 'люби́ти' gives 'люблю́' and 'лю́блять'. The other four forms keep the plain stem: 'ро́биш', 'ро́бить', 'ро́бимо', 'ро́бите'. Compare 'писа́ти' in the first conjugation, where the 'ш' runs through every form.

The infinitive tells you which conjugation to expect:

- Most verbs in '-ити' are second conjugation: 'говори́ти', 'роби́ти', 'люби́ти'.
- The exception is a verb in '-ити' with only one syllable before '-ти', such as 'жи́ти': it is first conjugation.
- Most verbs in '-ати', '-яти' and '-ува́ти' are first conjugation: 'чита́ти', 'писа́ти', 'працюва́ти'. 'Стоя́ти' is an exception.
- Verbs in '-іти' are divided: 'розумі́ти' is first conjugation ('розумі́єш'), and 'горі́ти', to burn, is second ('гори́ш').

The 'ти' form settles the question. An 'е' or 'є' in its ending ('пи́шеш', 'чита́єш') means the first conjugation; an 'и' or 'ї' ('ро́биш', 'гово́риш') means the second.

Stress in the present cannot be predicted from the infinitive, but it follows one of three patterns, and the 'я' and 'ти' forms show which one:

- On the stem in every form: 'чита́ю', 'чита́єш'; 'працю́ю', 'працю́єш'.
- On the ending in every form: 'живу́', 'живе́ш', and in 'живемо́', 'живете́' on the last syllable.
- On the ending in the 'я' form only, and on the stem from the 'ти' form on: 'пишу́', 'пи́шеш'; 'роблю́', 'ро́биш'; 'люблю́', 'лю́биш'; 'говорю́', 'гово́риш'.

When the 'я' and 'ти' forms are stressed in the same place, so is the whole tense. When they differ, the 'ти' form shows the stress of all the other forms.

grammar.title: How, how well and why: adverbs, 'люби́ти' with an infinitive, and 'тому́ що'
grammar.explanation:
An adverb is a word that tells how, when, where or how much something happens: 'до́бре', 'сього́дні', 'тут', 'ду́же'. Many adverbs of manner, which say how something is done, are made from adjectives by replacing the ending '-ий' with '-о', or in a few words with '-е':

- 'шви́дкий', quick, gives 'шви́дко'
- 'пові́льний', slow, gives 'пові́льно'
- 'пога́ний', bad, gives 'пога́но'
- 'до́брий', good, as in 'до́брий день', gives 'до́бре'

An adverb never changes its form. It describes an action, a quality or another adverb, never a noun, so it has no gender, number or case. Adverbs of degree say how much: 'ду́же', very or very much, and 'тро́хи', a little. 'Ду́же' goes before an adjective or adverb ('ду́же пові́льно', very slowly) and before a verb ('Я ду́же люблю́ чита́ти.', I really love reading).

In a neutral sentence the adverb usually stands just before the verb: 'Я до́бре розумі́ю.', literally 'I well understand', where English says 'I understand well'. Because Ukrainian puts the new or important information last (unit 5), 'Він гово́рить шви́дко.' puts the weight on how fast he speaks. Both orders are correct.

'Люби́ти' with an infinitive says what you love or like doing: 'Я люблю́ чита́ти.', literally 'I love to-read', where English says 'I love reading'. Only 'люби́ти' changes for the person; the infinitive stays as it is.

'Як?' asks how and 'Чому́?' asks why. The answer to 'Чому́?' begins with 'тому́ що', because. 'Тому́' on its own means 'for that reason', and 'що' is the word for 'what', which also joins one statement to another as English 'that' does. Together they work as one conjunction, a word that joins words or statements, like 'і', 'а' and 'але́'. Inside a sentence a comma goes before it: 'Я чита́ю, тому́ що люблю́ чита́ти.'

To say which language someone speaks, writes or reads, Ukrainian puts 'украї́нською' or 'англі́йською' after the verb: 'Я говорю́ украї́нською.', literally 'I speak by-Ukrainian'. These words are not adverbs. Each is a form of an adjective, 'украї́нський' or 'англі́йський', in the instrumental case, the case of the means by which something is done (unit 5). It is feminine because it agrees with the feminine noun 'мо́ва', language, which is left out: the full phrase is 'украї́нською мо́вою', 'by-Ukrainian by-language'. Learn the two forms whole for now; a later unit teaches the instrumental.

rows: Чому́? Тому́ що я тут живу́.
why? for-that-reason that I here live.

examples.target: Чому́ ти пи́шеш пові́льно? Тому́ що ду́маю.
examples.source: Why do you write slowly? Because I'm thinking.
examples.source_literal: why you write slowly? for-that-reason that I-think.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the new verb forms and adverbs
grammar.explanation:
The new words of this unit follow the rules of the first four units, with one small addition for 'украї́нською'. The points worth a close look are these.

'Працю́ю' has two letters 'ю' with two different jobs (unit 3). The first follows the consonant 'ц', so it makes the 'ц' soft and gives only the vowel [u]. The second follows a vowel, so it is [j] plus [u]. The stress moves from the 'а' of 'працюва́ти' to the 'ю' of the new stem and stays there in every present form. The same [j] is heard in every first-conjugation ending after a vowel: 'чита́ю', 'зна́єш', 'розумі́є'.

In 'роблю́' and 'ро́блять' the 'б' stays hard, and the added 'л' is soft, because 'ю' and 'я' follow it. The 'ь' at the end of 'ро́блять', 'гово́рить' and 'працю́ють' makes the 'т' soft; it has no sound of its own.

'Живу́' shows the full present stem 'жив-'. The 'в' stands before a vowel, so it is [ʋ], not the [w] it becomes at the end of a syllable. The 'ж' is hard before 'и', and the 'и' is [ɪ].

In 'пишу́' the 'ш' replaces the 'с' of 'писа́ти'. The stress moves from the ending of 'пишу́' to the stem of 'пи́шеш', and the unstressed 'е' of the ending '-еш' moves a little toward 'и' (unit 4). The stress moves the same way between 'роблю́' and 'ро́биш', and between 'люблю́' and 'лю́биш'.

In 'украї́нською' the 'ї' is always [ji], the 'ь' makes the 'с' soft, and the final 'ю' follows a vowel, so it is [ju]. The addition is that in speech the 'н' before that soft 'с' becomes soft as well. 'Англі́йською' has the same ending, with 'й' [j] before the 'с'.

In 'пові́льно' the 'ь' makes the 'л' soft, and the 'н' after it is hard before 'о'. In 'шви́дко' the 'д' stays voiced before 'к', and in 'за́раз' the final 'з' stays [z], because Ukrainian keeps voiced consonants voiced (unit 2). 'Що' in 'тому́ що' is [ʃt͡ʃɔ], as always.

rows: First 'ю' softens 'ц'; second 'ю' follows a vowel, so [ju]
Added 'л' again; stress on the stem

culture.title: Ukrainian and English at work and in daily life
culture.text:
Ukrainian is the state language of Ukraine. The constitution names it, and a law passed in 2019 makes it the language of government, education and public life. Since 2021 the same law has required shops, cafés and other services to serve customers in Ukrainian by default; a customer may ask to be served in another language. So a visitor who says 'До́брий день' is answered in Ukrainian, and the next sentences are often the ones from this unit:

- 'Ви гово́рите англі́йською?', do you speak English?
- 'Я тро́хи говорю́ украї́нською.', I speak a little Ukrainian.
- 'Я не розумі́ю.', I don't understand.

Ukrainians are usually pleased when a foreigner tries to speak Ukrainian, however slowly, and 'Ви до́бре гово́рите украї́нською!', you speak Ukrainian well, is a compliment learners hear often.

English is the foreign language most Ukrainian children learn at school, and many younger people speak it well. Ukraine also has a large information technology industry, with many companies in Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv and Dnipro working for clients abroad. Programmers like Taras often write and read English all day and speak Ukrainian with their colleagues, exactly as he describes. Colleagues of a similar age usually say 'ти' to each other, while a manager or a client is addressed with 'ви' until they suggest otherwise.

exercises.prompt: Match each Ukrainian verb with its meaning
Which sentence means 'I understand a little'?
exercises.explanation: 'Тро́хи' means 'a little' and 'розумі́ю' is the 'я' form of 'розумі́ти', to understand. 'До́бре' is 'well', 'пога́но' is 'badly', and 'пишу́' is 'I write'.
'Чита́ти' is first conjugation and its stem 'чита-' ends in a vowel, so the 'ми' ending is spelled '-ємо'.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences can 'Я чита́ю.' translate?
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian has one present tense for both English presents. Context, or a word such as 'за́раз', shows that the action is happening now.
The suffix '-юва-' becomes '-ю-', and after that vowel the 'вони́' ending of the first conjugation is spelled '-ють'.
'Жи́ти' has the present stem 'жив-', a consonant, so the 'ми' ending is '-емо', and the stress stays on the ending.

exercises.prompt: Which form of a verb tells you for certain which conjugation it follows?
exercises.explanation: An 'е' or 'є' in the 'ти' ending means the first conjugation, an 'и' or 'ї' the second. The infinitive only suggests the conjugation, and the 'я' endings look the same in both.
'Писа́ти' changes 'с' to 'ш' in the present, and its 'я' form is stressed on the ending.

exercises.prompt: 'Ду́мати' gives 'ти ду́маєш'. Which conjugation does it follow?
choices: The second, because the infinitive ends in '-ти'
The first, because the 'ти' ending has 'є'
The second, because the 'ти' ending has 'є'
exercises.explanation: Every infinitive ends in '-ти', so that tells you nothing. The 'є' of '-єш' marks the first conjugation; the second would have 'и'.
'Говори́ти' is second conjugation, so the 'вони́' ending is '-ять', with the stress on the stem as in 'гово́риш'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'роблю́' have an 'л' that 'ро́биш' does not?
choices: Every 'я' form of every verb adds 'л'
The 'л' shows where the stress falls
'б' cannot be fully soft, so the 'я' and 'вони́' forms add a soft 'л' after it
exercises.explanation: The 'я' and 'вони́' endings of the second conjugation make the consonant before them soft. 'Б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' cannot be fully soft, so an 'л' is added and takes the softness. The other forms keep the plain stem.

exercises.prompt: In 'працю́ю', what do the two letters 'ю' stand for?
choices: [u] after a soft 'ц', then [j] plus [u] after a vowel
exercises.explanation: After a consonant, 'ю' makes the consonant soft and gives only [u]. After a vowel, it writes [j] plus [u], the same [j] heard in 'чита́ю'.
'Люби́ти' is second conjugation with a stem ending in 'б', so its 'я' form adds 'л': 'люблю́'. The infinitive 'чита́ти' after it does not change.

exercises.prompt: In which present forms of 'писа́ти' does 'ш' replace the 'с'?
exercises.explanation: In the first conjugation a changed stem runs through the whole present: 'пишу́', 'пи́шеш', 'пи́шуть'. The added 'л' of the second conjugation is the change limited to the 'я' and 'вони́' forms.

exercises.hint_source: What are you doing? (to your teacher)
exercises.explanation: A teacher is addressed with 'ви'. 'Роби́ти' is second conjugation, so the 'ви' ending is '-ите', and the 'л' appears only in the 'я' and 'вони́' forms.

exercises.prompt: 'Пишу́' is stressed on the ending and 'пи́шеш' on the stem. Where is the stress in the 'ми', 'ви' and 'вони́' forms?
choices: On the ending, as in the 'я' form
On the stem, as in the 'ти' form
exercises.explanation: When the 'я' and 'ти' forms are stressed in different places, the 'ти' form shows the stress of all the other forms: 'пи́шемо', 'пи́шете', 'пи́шуть'.
'Пові́льно', slowly, is the adverb made from 'пові́льний'. In a neutral sentence it stands before the verb.

exercises.prompt: What does 'говори́ти украї́нською' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: 'Украї́нською' is the instrumental feminine of the adjective 'украї́нський', agreeing with 'мо́вою', by language, which is left out. It is an adjective form, not an adverb.

exercises.prompt_target: Я не розумі́ю, ___ що ти шви́дко гово́риш.
exercises.hint_source: I don't understand, because you speak quickly.
exercises.explanation: 'Тому́ що' is the conjunction 'because', and a comma goes before it inside a sentence.
'Жи́ти' gives 'живу́'. After the vowel of 'живу́', the preposition is 'в'.
The 'вона́' form of 'писа́ти' is 'пи́ше'. The adverb can stand before the verb or, with more weight, after it.

exercises.prompt_source: Why are you reading? (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: A friend is addressed with 'ти', and the 'ти' form of 'чита́ти' is 'чита́єш'.

exercises.prompt_source: I write slowly because I'm thinking.
Do you speak English? (to a stranger)
exercises.explanation: A stranger is addressed with 'ви', and the 'ви' form of 'говори́ти' is 'гово́рите'.
